title: A Preregistered Audit of Dataset Contamination Controls in LLM-for-NetOps Benchmarks
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired, confirmatory audit that tested whether conservative deterministic contamination detectors (exact‑match + fuzzy 5‑gram + provenance heuristics) flag items in a reproducible 150‑item NetOps sample and whether applying preregistered contamination controls changes validator‑based success rates. Under preregistration study_id = contamination-audit-netops-2026-v1 we ran 150 item pairs (baseline vs guarded) using a single hosted model (declared_model_version = "gpt-5-mini") with shared_initial_candidate generation semantics and a deterministic NetOps validator. The preregistered detectors produced zero high‑confidence contamination flags and no guarded exclusions were applied. All 150 baseline episodes and their matched guarded episodes passed the validator (baseline = 150/150, guarded = 150/150). The paired success‑rate difference = 0.0 percentage points (95% CI [0.0, 0.0]); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. We reconcile preregistration→execution artifacts, explain why the outcome is degenerate (provenance‑stable synthetic sampling + shared generation semantics), report execution accounting and deterministically archived traces, and provide concrete, artifact‑grounded recommendations to increase audit sensitivity in future work.

sections.introduction:
Motivation and problem statement. Large language models are increasingly proposed to translate high‑level operational intent into device configuration artifacts and to propose automated repairs. Adoption for production NetOps requires rigorous evaluation practices that are contamination‑aware and construct‑valid: if benchmark items overlap model training data (contamination) or are templated/low‑complexity, reported accuracy may be inflated and operational risk underestimated. Recent surveys and system papers emphasize both the promise and the evaluation risks of LLM‑for‑NetOps research. To address a targeted methodological question in this space we preregistered a confirmatory audit that operationalizes conservative, deterministic contamination detectors and a guarded exclusion policy, then measures whether applying those controls changes a validator‑based success rate on a reproducible 150‑item sample.

Research question and contribution. Our preregistered research question asks: after freezing deterministic contamination‑detection and treatment rules, how many high‑confidence contamination flags occur in a reproducible 150‑item sample, and how much does applying those controls change an LLM's validator pass rate? We contribute: (1) a fully preregistered, archived paired confirmatory experiment (study_id = contamination-audit-netops-2026-v1) executed end‑to‑end under the frozen plan; (2) exact, artifact‑verified confirmatory statistics on Npairs = 150 with deterministic validator traces and analysis artifacts; and (3) a preregistration→execution reconciliation that explains the observed degenerate null and prescribes stronger future audit designs. Importantly, the executed sample for this run used provenance‑stable synthetic tasks generated by the deterministic task generator described in the preregistration; the execution also used shared_initial_candidate generation semantics such that a single model generation per item was reused for both baseline and guarded episodes in the absence of high‑confidence flags. These two execution facts materially limit the present run's sensitivity to detect generation‑level contamination effects; we make this limitation explicit in the Abstract, Introduction, Methods, Results, Discussion, and Disclosure Statement and anchor each statement to archived artifacts.
sections.related_work:
LLM‑driven NetOps research and benchmarks. Prior empirical work demonstrates that LLMs can translate intent into configuration artifacts in constrained settings and that agentic and validate–repair architectures typically improve average repair quality versus naive generation (recent benchmark and system papers summarized by contemporary surveys). Deterministic network verifiers based on header‑space analysis and related formal frameworks are a standard way to check reachability and policy properties and therefore serve as practical oracles in produce–validate evaluations. Recent benchmark studies and system projects also document regressions and scale sensitivity for LLM repair and emphasize that integrating formal verification or iterative validate–repair loops improves measured reliability.

Evaluation validity and contamination concerns. Meta‑evaluations and methodological surveys highlight contamination and construct‑validity risks for LLM benchmarks: public, web‑crawled corpora may contain near‑identical or templated items that leak into model training data; evaluation protocols lacking provenance tracing and n‑gram overlap checks are vulnerable to inflated accuracy. These methodological critiques motivated our preregistered contamination detectors (exact normalized token equality; fuzzy 5‑gram shingle overlap with preregistered thresholds; provenance timestamp heuristics) and the guarded exclusion policy that deterministically replaces high‑confidence flagged items. Our audit deliberately operationalizes a conservative subset of recommended defenses from that literature and then measures their effect in a reproducible execution.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimands. The experiment was preregistered as contamination-audit-netops-2026-v1. The primary estimand is the paired success‑rate difference (guarded − baseline) computed across item×model pairs and tested by an exact McNemar two‑sided test. A paired bootstrap percentile 95% confidence interval was computed with 10,000 resamples using seed = 1729. The confirmatory sample size was 150 item pairs (planned_episode_count = 300 episodes). The preregistration specified conservative contamination detectors and a guarded treatment that deterministically excludes only high‑confidence flagged items (exact match OR fuzzy 5‑gram overlap ≥ 0.80) and replaces them with deterministic retemplated/topology‑augmented items sampled from the same generator distribution using fixed seeds.

Detectors and validator (archive‑grounded). The preregistered detectors were: (1) exact normalized token equality after whitespace and token canonicalization; (2) 5‑gram shingle fuzzy overlap (Jaccard/overlap) with preregistered thresholds (high‑confidence ≥ 0.80; lower bands noted for sensitivity analysis); and (3) metadata provenance heuristics comparing item timestamps to model cutoff. The verification oracle is deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (validator traces and pass/fail codes are archived). The analysis executor used is paired_binary_analysis_v1; analysis inputs and outputs are archived and their SHA‑256 identifiers are recorded in the execution bundle.

Sampling and generation semantics (critical preregistration→execution detail). The preregistration allowed deterministic replacement sampling and permitted controlled task generators where necessary. The executed run used a deterministic task generator (deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5) that produced provenance‑stable synthetic items (source_identifier prefix "synthetic-netops:") as the confirmatory sample. Execution semantics set independent_condition_generation = false (shared_initial_candidate semantics) so a single shared generation was produced per item and reused for both baseline and guarded episodes when no high‑confidence exclusions occurred. Because high‑confidence flags were not produced, the shared generation semantics reduced actual model calls to one per item (model_calls_used = 150) rather than two. The execution manifest and deterministic_reconciliation artifacts confirm these settings and counts.

Planned analysis and sensitivity. The preregistration specified the primary confirmatory test above and two prespecified sensitivity analyses: (a) complete_pair_primary_with_failure_as_zero_sensitivity (treating failed model calls as failures), and (b) fuzzy‑threshold sensitivity (evaluating thresholds 0.50, 0.65, 0.80). The preregistration included power and precision planning guidance: the original multi‑model design aimed to detect ≈5 percentage‑point paired differences with 80% power at α=0.05; the single‑model single‑call execution executed here has correspondingly larger minimal detectable effects. All analysis parameters (bootstrap resamples, seed, and executor identifiers) are archived in analysis/analysis_log.jsonl and in the analysis results artifact.
sections.results:
Execution accounting and deterministic reconciliation. The execution completed all planned episodes: planned_episode_count = 300; completed_episode_count = 300; failed_episode_count = 0. Because independent_condition_generation = false and no high‑confidence exclusions were triggered, model_calls_used = 150 (one shared generation per item). The deterministic_reconciliation artifact confirms complete_pair_count = 150, n_11 = 150, n_10 = 0, n_01 = 0, n_00 = 0 and that provider call accounting and cache metrics are consistent with the preregistered execution contract.

Contamination detection outcomes. The preregistered detectors produced zero high‑confidence contamination flags on the executed sample. The archived contamination summary (analysis/contamination_summary.csv) contains no flagged episodes (file content empty apart from header). Because no high‑confidence flags occurred, the guarded policy performed no exclusions or deterministic replacements; this is reflected in the execution bundle and in the transformation_manifest and task_manifest artifacts which show no replacement entries for flagged items.

Validator scoring and confirmatory statistics. The deterministic_netops_validator_v5 returned pass for all baseline episodes (baseline_success_count = 150/150; baseline_success_rate = 1.0) and for all guarded episodes (guarded_success_count = 150/150; guarded_success_rate = 1.0). The paired contingency table is n11 = 150, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0 (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv). The primary estimand (paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline) = 0.0 percentage points. Paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, bootstrap_seed = 1729) = [0.0, 0.0]. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. All these numeric outcomes and the underlying per‑episode validator traces and raw responses are archived and referenced in the execution manifest (representative artifact hashes are recorded in the Disclosure Statement).

Absence of numeric fuzzy‑overlap summaries. The preregistered detectors include fuzzy 5‑gram overlap checks, but the archived contamination_summary.csv contains no per‑item overlap scores for the executed sample (it is empty of flagged entries). The absence of high‑confidence flags means there were no recorded episodes requiring deterministic replacement under the preregistered rules; the detector logs archived in the bundle therefore do not contain an aggregated distribution of overlap scores to report here. We explicitly report this archive‑grounded absence rather than inventing summary statistics: the execution bundle documents zero high‑confidence flags and contains the contamination_summary.csv artifact (SHA‑256 recorded) that substantiates this statement.

Representative artifacts and reproducibility accounting. Representative per‑task shared_initial responses, baseline responses, guarded responses, and validator traces are archived (execution/responses and execution/scoring subpaths). The analysis input/results SHA‑256 (analysis input/results) and representative artifact SHAs (execution/model_configuration.json, execution/task_manifest.jsonl, analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv, analysis/contamination_summary.csv) are recorded in the Disclosure Statement. The analysis log records bootstrap parameters and confirms the resampling run; the deterministic_reconciliation artifact confirms pair and episode accounting consistency.
sections.discussion:
Interpreting the degenerate null. The degenerate outcome (perfect agreement: all pairs pass) is artifact‑backed and arises from two nonexclusive execution facts recorded in the archive: (1) the sampled items were provenance‑stable synthetic tasks produced by a deterministic generator (source_identifier prefix "synthetic-netops:") so exact/fuzzy high‑confidence matches to public corpus fingerprints did not occur under the preregistered thresholds; and (2) shared_initial_candidate semantics (independent_condition_generation = false) produced a single shared generation per item that, in the absence of exclusions, produced identical baseline and guarded episodes. Both facts are present in the archived task_manifest, transformation manifest, and deterministic_reconciliation artifacts and therefore constitute the mechanistic explanation for the null effect. Because these execution facts were permitted by the preregistration and no post‑hoc changes to exclusion rules occurred, the analysis artifacts record no deviations_from_preregistration.

What this execution answers (and what it does not). This execution answers a constrained, preregistered question: given provenance‑stable synthetic sampling and conservative deterministic detectors, do high‑confidence flags arise and do deterministic guarded exclusions change validator pass rates? For this particular synthetic sample and generation semantics, the answer is: no high‑confidence flags were produced and no change in validator pass rate was observed. This result does not generalize to web‑sourced public benchmarks, to detectors that report paraphrase‑level overlaps, to independent regeneration semantics, or to other LLM families and model sizes. We explicitly avoid making broader contamination prevalence claims about public benchmarks; such claims require provenance‑rich public sampling, paraphrase‑robust detectors, human adjudication, and larger/multi‑model designs.

Design lessons and concrete recommendations. The artifact‑grounded cause of the null suggests practical audit improvements that follow directly from the preregistration and execution artifacts: (1) sample provenance‑rich public items (avoid relying exclusively on deterministic synthetic generators when the audit's objective is to detect contamination in web‑sourced benchmarks); (2) set independent_condition_generation = true to produce independent baseline and guarded generations per item (this prevents single shared generations collapsing paired comparisons); (3) expand to multiple models and multiple independent seeds to increase observable discordance; (4) layer paraphrase/paraphrase‑robust detectors and human adjudication for borderline flags (the preregistration anticipated fuzzy‑threshold sensitivity analyses but archive evidence here shows no flags triggered that workflow); and (5) align sample size to a targeted minimal detectable paired effect using explicit power calculations appropriate to the design (the preregistration contains sensitivity guidance showing that single‑model single‑call designs have reduced sensitivity versus multi‑model designs). These recommendations are supported by the archived execution artifacts and the preregistration power discussion.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered, artifact‑anchored paired audit of conservative contamination detectors for LLM‑for‑NetOps evaluation. In the reproducible 150‑pair synthetic sample we observed zero preregistered high‑confidence contamination flags and identical validator pass rates (150/150 baseline, 150/150 guarded). The degenerate null is artifact‑supported and stems from provenance‑stable synthetic sampling and shared generation semantics; it does not imply the absence of contamination in web‑sourced benchmarks nor the general failure of the preregistered detectors in other sampling regimes. We provide explicit preregistration→execution reconciliation, confirm that deterministic reconciliation checks passed, and recommend concrete design changes (provenance‑rich sampling, independent generation, multi‑model scope, paraphrase‑sensitive detectors, and matched power calculations) to increase audit sensitivity in future work.

limitations: Single‑model execution (gpt‑5-mini) — results do not generalize across other LLM families, sizes, or training corpora.

Sampled items were provenance‑stable synthetic/deterministically generated tasks (source_identifier prefix "synthetic-netops:") for this run; absence of high‑confidence flags here may not reflect contamination prevalence in real‑world, web‑crawled benchmarks.

Generation semantics used shared_initial_candidate across baseline and guarded conditions (independent_condition_generation = false), producing identical model outputs when no exclusions occurred and thus limiting sensitivity to interventions that rely on independent re‑generation.

Contamination detection relied on preregistered conservative heuristics (exact match and fuzzy 5‑gram overlap thresholds); subtler contamination patterns (paraphrased memorization, partial leakage) may escape these heuristics and require richer provenance or manual adjudication.

Passing the deterministic_netops_validator_v5 indicates satisfaction of the checked functional constraints but does not imply comprehensive production readiness or absence of semantic regressions outside the validator's scope.
